source.title: Superfiltering: Weak-to-Strong Data Filtering for Fast Instruction-Tuning
source.authors: Ming Li; Yong Zhang; Shwai He; Zhitao Li; Hongyu Zhao; Jian-Zong Wang; Ning Cheng; Tian-Yi Zhou

page_placements.theme: Small models select training data or tokens for larger models

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper applies a weak-to-strong idea to instruction-data filtering and reports results, but it does not test whether a strong student trained on weak-model labels beats the weak labeler.
record.gate_note: The paper uses GPT-2 to rank and select instruction data, then fine-tunes LLaMA2 on that selected data. This is not fine-tuning on labels produced by the weaker model, and its comparisons are not PGR or performance against a weak supervisor. Results are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: GPT-2 does not label anything. It scores existing instruction-response pairs (IFD), and LLaMA2 is fine-tuned on the selected original responses. There are no weak-model labels, no weak-supervisor task performance and no PGR. The comparisons are against full-data fine-tuning and other data filters. The paper only notes a 'similar spirit' to Burns et al. So it neither tests nor uses the weak-to-strong finding. It is T6, not T3, because no result bears on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Weak and strong LMs rank instruction difficulty consistently, so GPT-2 can filter data for LLaMA2 instruction tuning about 20x faster, with equal or better results than full-data tuning. The authors also concede that filtering with LLaMA2-7B itself performs better (Tables 3-4).
record.recipe_differences: GPT-2 computes IFD scores to select existing instruction-response examples; LLaMA2 is fine-tuned on those examples. The weak model does not generate the training labels used for student fine-tuning.
record.method_sensitivity: Filtering rankings and overlap vary by model, dataset, metric, and selection budget; fine-tuned-model outcomes vary by dataset, student size, and selected-data ratio.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT-2's perplexity and IFD rankings correlate with LLaMA2-7B's (Spearman about 0.68-0.80). Overlap of the selected subsets rises from about 0.24-0.42 at 5% to 0.49-0.61 at 15%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A small pretrained LM can proxy a larger LM when ranking instruction data by difficulty.

fits_no_version.finding: LLaMA2-7B/13B fine-tuned on GPT-2-selected 5-15% subsets get pairwise winning scores of 1.014-1.193 against full-data models. Human majority vote at 5% is 50/18/32 (Alpaca) and 49/5/46 (Alpaca-GPT4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small-model data filtering can match or beat full-data instruction tuning of a larger model.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The authors note that experiments cover 3 datasets and 2 LLaMA2 base models and recommend broader evaluation. The reported comparisons do not measure the weak model's task performance or PGR, and uncertainty estimates for the listed results are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 results for GPT-2-large, GPT-2-XL, and GPT-NEO; other Table 2 benchmark columns; and Table 3 ablations comparing data-selection strategies and filter models were left out. They concern filtering consistency or filtering-method performance and do not measure the weak-label student-versus-supervisor effect.

untested.parts: No student trained on weak-model labels; no weak-supervisor performance or PGR.
No training change to weak-label fine-tuning. The ablations compare data-selection strategies and filter models.
Filter size is varied (GPT-2 to LLaMA2-7B, Tables 1 and 3), but only for ranking agreement and selected-data performance, not PGR.
No checkability, distribution-shift or error-overlap tests on weak-label training.

record.verdict_notes: The rows record the study's own method against baselines; this is appropriate only as fits_no_version material, and all rows correctly carry versions ['none']. The paper misdescribes Burns et al. as finetuning GPT-4 on 'weaker ChatGPT' data. The text says results are 'shown in Table 5' when it means Table 2. 'Weak-to-strong' here names a filtering proxy, not supervision, so this study should not be counted as evidence for any version.

versions.untested_parts: The student is not trained on weak-model-produced labels; no weak-supervisor performance or PGR is reported.
The paper compares data-selection strategies and filter models, not training changes to weak-label fine-tuning.
It studies model-size and dataset differences for filtering consistency, not how those factors affect PGR across NLP, chess, or reward modelling.
It does not test supervisor-checkability, distribution shift in weak-label training, or error overlap between weak and strong models.
No theory of when a student must outperform its supervisor is tested.

relation.reason: The introduction and Section 7.2 discuss Burns et al.'s weak supervision as related work; the study's experiments evaluate data filtering.

tranche.reason: The study measures ranking consistency and instruction tuning on filtered existing responses. It neither tests nor uses the claim that students trained on weaker-model labels outperform their supervisors.

source_check.notes: GPT-2 scores existing responses rather than generating student training labels; no supervisor-performance comparison or PGR is reported. Pairwise winning scores equal 1 + (wins − losses)/all comparisons, not win rates.
